message.content:
Below is a concise summary of your key rights and protections under Texas residential‑tenancy law (Texas Property Code §§ 92–99). These apply whether you’re renting a single‑family home, apartment unit, townhouse, condo, mobile home, or other dwelling: | Category | Your Rights | |----------|-------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent if the lease specifies it.
• Must return deposit within 30 days after tenancy ends unless deductions are made for unpaid rent, damages beyond normal wear & tear, or cleaning costs.
• Deductions must be itemized and sent with the remaining balance. | | **Habitability / Repairs** | • Landlords must keep premises safe, sanitary, and fit for habitation—plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, pest control, etc.
• If repairs aren’t done promptly, you have the right to request them in writing. After repeated failure, you may file a complaint with local code enforcement or seek court action. | | **Rent Increases** | • For most leases, landlords cannot raise rent without giving at least 90 days’ written notice before the increase takes effect.
• Some cities impose limits on how much rent can rise per year (e.g., Houston has a “rent‑control” ordinance limiting increases to 5% annually). Check city ordinances where applicable. | | **Entry Notice** | • Landlords must give *reasonable* notice (usually 24 hours) before entering except in emergencies. They may enter during reasonable times (typically daytime). | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live peacefully without unreasonable interference from the landlord or others they bring onto the property. | | **Discrimination Protections** | • Under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas statutes, landlords cannot discriminate against tenants based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, age, marital status, source of income, or military service. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with proper notice (normally 30 days).
• Tenants who pay rent on time and follow lease terms generally receive full refund of security deposits upon move‑out. | | **Eviction Process** | • Evictions require a formal lawsuit filed in county district court. A judge will issue a writ of possession only after a judgment is entered.
• Common grounds include nonpayment of rent, violation of lease terms, illegal activity, or owner’s intent to occupy the unit personally. | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct Option** *(limited)* | • Texas does not allow repair‑and‑deduct for habitability issues like mold or pests. Instead, tenants must notify the landlord first and wait a reasonable period for remediation. | ### Practical Steps When Issues Arise 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of all communications (emails, texts), photos/video evidence of problems, receipts for any out‑of‑pocket expenses related to maintenance, and records of rent payments. 2. **Written Requests** – Send a certified mail or email requesting repairs or addressing concerns. Include dates, descriptions, and reference relevant sections of the Texas Property Code. 3. **Local Ordinance Checks** – Many Texas municipalities enforce stricter rules than state law (e.g., minimum housing standards, eviction timelines). Verify local codes through city clerk offices or official websites. 4. **Seek Mediation** – Before filing suit, consider mediation services offered by many counties or nonprofit organizations. It often resolves disputes faster and cheaper. 5. **Legal Aid Resources** - **Texan Legal Services** – Offers free or low‑cost representation for qualifying residents. - **Houston Tenant Union**, **Dallas Renters Alliance**, etc.—local groups providing guidance and advocacy. --- #### Quick Reference Checklist - [ ] Lease signed? Review its clauses carefully. - [ ] Security deposit returned? Confirm amount and reasons for deduction. - [ ] Maintenance requests logged? Follow up if unresolved > 7 days. - [ ] Received notice of rent increase? Ensure it meets 90‑day requirement. - [ ] Landlord entry? Was there adequate notice? - [ ] Discriminatory behavior observed? Document incidents. If you encounter a problem that isn’t resolved via communication or mediation, consult a qualified attorney specializing in landlord‑tenant law. They can advise on potential claims such as breach of covenant, unlawful detainer defense, or statutory violations.
